title: M54, NGC 6715
caption: The globular cluster M54, imaged by the KPNO 0.9-meter telescope

recognition.text: Published in the NSF NOIRLab image archive. No published rating.

story: This composite shows M54, also cataloged as NGC 6715, a globular cluster in Sagittarius. It appears bright but small on the sky, and its crowded core is too dense for this telescope to split into separate stars.

A globular cluster is a tightly packed ball of old stars, held together by their combined gravity. Most globular clusters orbit our own Milky Way, and for a long time M54 was assumed to be one of them, at a distance of some 60000 light-years.

There is now a claim that M54 actually belongs to another galaxy altogether, the Sagittarius Dwarf, which is a small member of the Local Group, the collection of galaxies that includes the Milky Way. If so, M54 would lie nearly 90000 light-years away, making it a visitor from outside our Galaxy that only appears to sit among Sagittarius's stars.
scale: M54 was long thought to be about 60000 light-years away, though if it belongs to the Sagittarius Dwarf it would be nearly 90000 light-years away, according to NOIRLab.

understand.summary: The 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak recorded M54 in visible light, and the images were combined into a composite. The filters and color mapping are not published.
understand.eye: The telescope's exposures separate the cluster's outer stars, though even this camera cannot resolve the densely packed core.

explore: The images for this composite were taken in July 1998 with the 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory, as part of the Research Experiences for Undergraduates program there, supported by the National Science Foundation. The field is 11.6 arcminutes across.
alt: A small, bright ball of stars with an unresolved central glow.
